title: Why Trial And Error Is Bad For Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/05/17/why-trial-and-error-is-bad-for-difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that difficult students are frequently subjected to a shifting, inconsistent parade of strategies—behavior contracts, special privileges, harsh consequences, excessive praise—that deepens rather than resolves their struggles. He describes this trial-and-error cycle as confusing and destructive, reinforcing a student's sense of being different, damaged, and less capable than peers. His central claim is that it isn't any particular strategy that transforms difficult students' behavior, but the steady, fair, consistent presence of a trusted teacher: predictable accountability, warmth, and genuine rapport applied every single day. He calls on teachers to stop the cycle of 'strategy of the week' experimentation and instead build a stable environment from the first day of school, arguing that consistency itself, sustained over time, is what changes behavior.
points: Difficult students are often subjected to a rotating, inconsistent parade of contracts, incentives, and consequences ('strategy of the week').
This trial-and-error cycle reinforces a student's sense of being different, damaged, or less capable than peers.
It's not any single strategy but the steady, fair, day-after-day presence of a trusted teacher that transforms behavior.
Fair and consistent accountability, combined with humor and rapport, is described as the real engine of change.
Teachers are urged to build a stable environment from the first day of school rather than experimenting after problems appear.
quotes: They need your fixed boundaries, your steady, predictable presence, your faithful accountability, and your commitment to doing what is right by them and their future.
What they often get, however, is something entirely different. What they often get is an endless succession of haphazard strategies.
One week their every move is corrected . The next week they’re ignored. The week after that they’re excessively praised.
It’s confusing and destructive. It labels them in the eyes of their peers and plays with their emotions.
The fact is, difficult students will never truly improve as long as they’re treated like test subjects. For it isn’t trial and error that transforms behavior.
It’s your fair and consistent accountability. It’s your humor and rapport. It’s the smiles, the gentleness, the mutual likability, and the heartfelt connection between you.
You have to create a stable environment they can count on—one you begin teaching, modeling, and implementing the first day of school .
